title: The beggar at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1–10)
hookLine: Peter has no money, so he gives what he has: the man walks, leaps, praises
carry: such as I have, give I thee

cards: You're coming out of a store and someone by the door asks for change. You pat your pockets. Nothing.
Who carries cash these days? So you do the little shrug, the half smile, and keep walking, not quite looking at them. Now the temple in Jerusalem, three in the afternoon, the hour of prayer.

Peter and John are walking up. At the gate called Beautiful, a man lies on the ground, unable to walk since birth. Every day someone carries him here, so he can ask the people going in to pray for a coin.
He sees Peter and John and asks. And Peter has no money either.

teach.h: LOOK ON US: FIRST, HE'S SEEN.
teach.b: First, Peter stops. He fixes his eyes on the man and says: look at us. Before anything else, the man is seen.
He looks up, expecting a coin.

teach.h: SILVER AND GOLD HAVE I NONE.
teach.b: And Peter says, in the King James Bible: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk."
He takes him by the right hand and lifts him up, and his feet and ankles grow strong.
Luke doesn't let him just stand there: "And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God."
Walking and leaping: the man carried to the door every day goes in through it on his own feet.
Peter doesn't pretend to have what he hasn't got, and he doesn't feel bad about the empty pockets and walk on. He gives what he actually has.

In the name of Jesus, for Christians, means by his authority and power, not Peter's: the story is careful that Peter isn't the healer. And the people who see it know this man; they've walked past him for years.
Where exactly was the Beautiful Gate? Nobody knows for certain: it's named nowhere else in the Bible, and scholars still debate which of the temple's gates it was.

teach.h: SUCH AS I HAVE GIVE I THEE.
teach.b: But the line has lasted: such as I have, give I thee.

how: Christians often quote Peter's words 'silver and gold have I none' when speaking about giving time, attention and care, and some churches' Sunday readings come from Acts 3 in the weeks after Easter.

o: the jeweled gate of heaven in Revelation
the gate where Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey
the temple gate where a man who couldn't walk begged

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: where the man was laid every day

he has none. he gives what he has: the name of Jesus, and his hand.
the man enters the temple with them
walking, and leaping, and praising God.

games.q: you're Peter, on your way to prayer. a man who has never walked asks you for money. you don't have any. what do you do?
o: stop, look at him, and give what you do have.
games.why: Peter says look on us, then: silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee. he takes his hand and lifts him up.

practice: Ask yourself, honestly, what you have today: maybe not money, maybe not energy, but perhaps ten minutes, a skill, a kind word, a good ear, the ability to look someone in the eye and say, I see you.
Pick one, and one person who could use it. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, just hold it ready.

wordCard.voice: Beautiful Gate. The temple entrance where a man who couldn't walk was laid every day to beg, until Peter took his hand and he went in leaping. This week: Emmaus, Thomas, a beach, a cloud, Pentecost, a shared table, and a gate.

orig.note: Greek: beautiful, timely, in its season. Acts calls the gate simply the one called Beautiful.

carryVoice: Your line: such as I have, give I thee. Tomorrow, a man who forgives as the stones fall. Eleven weeks on the path now.
